request.title: Why adding substrate eventually gives diminishing returns
request.topic: Explain to a first-year biology student why the initial reaction rate rises nearly proportionally at low substrate concentration but approaches a limiting rate at high substrate concentration, with total enzyme concentration held fixed. Use the simple Michaelis–Menten relation v = Vmax[S]/(Km + [S]) and connect its changing behavior to the meaning of Vmax and the half-maximum point [S] = Km. Make the relation between concentration and rate, the leveling off, and the half-maximum correspondence visually inspectable. Treat this as an idealized model under its usual initial-rate assumptions, not a claim that every enzyme follows it. Create exactly one continuous, coherent scene for a 35–45 second visual lesson with concise connected subtitle narration, roughly 75–95 words. Keep the main explanatory objects visible and use a useful interactive control only if it supports the explanation. No title card, unrelated recap, or decorative motion. Choose the visual representation best suited to the explanation.

request.title: How local coils become one folded protein
request.topic: Explain to a first-year biology student how a single long polypeptide can contain several local coiled regions that pack together into a compact tertiary structure. Create exactly two connected scenes totaling 70–90 seconds with concise connected subtitle narration, roughly 150–190 words across the lesson. In the first scene, establish the connected long chain, its local coils, and the intervening chain that joins them. In the second scene, carry the same chain and coils into a compact packed whole, showing how their arrangement contributes to tertiary structure. Preserve the chain and coil IDs, their visible identity, and chain continuity across the scene handoff so the student can track the same structure. Make both the local organization and overall packing inspectable. Clearly treat the sequence and motion as an explanatory schematic, not a deposited protein structure, a measured folding pathway, or a prediction of real folding dynamics.
